content: You are a coding agent working in a monorepo: Next.js frontend (web/), Express backend (server/), PostgreSQL 15. Run commands in the repo root and report results concisely.
SECURITY POLICY: Production authentication MUST use OAuth. API keys must not be used for production authentication.
Never commit .env files or any secrets to git. Do not print secret values in logs.
Prefer 2-space indentation and single quotes in TypeScript files.
Write commit messages with conventional prefixes (feat:, fix:, chore:) and keep them under 72 characters.
Let's start by checking the repo state. What branch are we on?
On `main`, clean working tree. Last commit: `chore: bump dependencies`. Three local branches: main, feat/navbar, feat/orders-api.
Create a branch for the orders API work.
Checked out `feat/orders-api` from main.
Add a GET /orders endpoint to the Express server that returns paginated orders.
Added `server/routes/orders.ts` with `GET /orders?page=&limit=`. Uses `LIMIT/OFFSET` against the orders table and returns `{ data, page, total }`.
The orders endpoint returns 500 when limit is missing.
Default `limit` was undefined and got passed into the SQL as NULL. Fixed by defaulting to 20 and clamping to 100.
Add zod validation to the orders query params.
Added `ordersQuerySchema` (page: int >= 1, limit: int 1..100). Invalid input now returns 400 with the zod issues array.
Now build the navbar for the web app.
Created `web/components/Navbar.tsx` with logo, links, and a Products dropdown. Styled with Tailwind.
The navbar looks broken on mobile, links overflow.
Added a hamburger toggle below the `md` breakpoint and collapsed the links into a vertical menu.
Make the navbar sticky.
Set `sticky top-0 z-50` on the header and added a backdrop blur with a bottom border.
The navbar dropdown flickers when I move the mouse from the button to the menu.
The gap between the button and the menu triggers `mouseleave` on the wrapper. Removed the 8px margin and used padding on the menu so the hover area is continuous.
Still flickering in Safari.
Safari fires `mouseleave` before `mouseenter` on the menu. Added a 120ms debounce on close and moved the dropdown into a portal so the hover target is stable.
Dropdown now stays open too long after leaving.
Reduced the close debounce to 60ms and cancel it on `mouseenter` of the menu. Verified the navbar dropdown no longer flickers in Chrome, Safari and Firefox.
The CSS for the navbar dropdown z-index is behind the hero section.
The hero had `position: relative; z-index: 60`. Lowered the hero to 10; the navbar dropdown at z-50 now stacks above it.
The Postgres migration for orders failed.
Migration 0007 errored: `relation "customers" does not exist`. The migration order was wrong; renamed it to run after 0005_create_customers.
Add an index on orders.created_at.
Added `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_created_at ON orders (created_at DESC)` in migration 0008.
The orders query is slow.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE showed a sequential scan on 2.1M rows. After the created_at index the query drops from 840ms to 12ms.
Now the server can't reach the database in docker compose.
Error: `connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432`. Inside compose the host should be `db`, not localhost. Updated DATABASE_URL to `postgres://app:app@db:5432/app`.
PostgreSQL connection failure again after restarting the containers.
Logs show `FATAL: the database system is starting up`. The server connected before Postgres finished recovery. Added a `pg_isready` healthcheck and `depends_on: condition: service_healthy`.
Sometimes we get 'too many connections' from Postgres under load.
The pool had `max: 100` per server instance with 4 instances. Reduced `max` to 10 per instance and set `idleTimeoutMillis: 30000`; connection errors stopped in the load test.
Also connection timeouts to Postgres on the staging box.
Staging security group blocked port 5432 from the app subnet. Opened it for the app subnet only; `SELECT 1` succeeds and the connection timeout is gone.
Run the unit tests.
`npm test`: 142 passed, 3 failed. Failures are in `orders.test.ts` (pagination defaults).
Fixed the test expectations to match the new default limit of 20. Re-ran: 145 passed.
Add tests for the zod validation.
Added 8 tests to `orders.validation.test.ts` covering missing, negative, and oversized params. All pass.
The Playwright e2e test for the navbar is flaky.
The test clicked before the dropdown animation finished. Replaced the fixed sleep with `await expect(menu).toBeVisible()`.
Run the production build.
`next build` failed: Type error in `web/app/orders/page.tsx:41` — Property 'total' does not exist on type 'Order[]'.
The API returns `{ data, page, total }` but the page typed it as `Order[]`. Introduced `Paginated<Order>` and updated the fetcher; build passes.
TypeScript complains about implicit any in the seed script.
`server/scripts/seed.ts(18,22): error TS7006: Parameter 'row' implicitly has an 'any' type.` Added an explicit `SeedRow` interface.
There is another TS error: Type 'string | undefined' is not assignable to type 'string'.
`process.env.DATABASE_URL` may be undefined. Added a `requireEnv()` helper that throws a clear error at startup.
Enable strict mode across the monorepo.
Set `strict: true` in the root tsconfig. Found 23 new errors, fixed 21 and left 2 with `// TODO` for the legacy billing module.

Staging is returning 502 intermittently.
nginx upstream timed out while a pod was terminating. Added a preStop sleep of 10s and `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30`. 502s gone.
Now let's do auth. Set up authentication for the API.
Scaffolded `server/auth/` with session middleware and a `/auth/login` route. Which scheme should production use?
Per the security policy, implemented OAuth 2.0 authorization-code flow with PKCE for production authentication using the `openid-client` library.
Configure the OAuth callback URL.

Set the OAuth redirect URI to `https://app.example.com/auth/callback` in the identity provider and `OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI` in the production config. Staging uses `https://staging.example.com/auth/callback`.
Login redirects back with an error.
Auth error: `invalid_grant: redirect_uri mismatch`. The provider had a trailing slash on the callback URL. Removed it and login succeeded.
Users get logged out after 15 minutes.
The OAuth access token expires in 900s and there was no refresh. Added refresh-token rotation in the auth middleware; sessions now last 8 hours.
We got a 401 Unauthorized on /orders in production.
The API was rejecting the bearer token because the audience claim did not match. Set `OAUTH_AUDIENCE=orders-api` in the production auth config.
For local development can I use an API key instead so I don't need the identity provider running?
Yes — for development only. Added a dev-only API key path enabled when `NODE_ENV=development`; it is compiled out of production builds so production authentication stays OAuth.
Add an auth test for the API key dev path.
Added `auth.devkey.test.ts` asserting the API key is accepted in development and rejected with 401 when `NODE_ENV=production`.
The auth middleware logs the token, is that ok?
No — removed the token from the logs and added a redaction filter for Authorization headers.
Internal note: the design system uses the Inter font and an 8px spacing grid.
Squash the last five commits before merging.
Interactive rebase isn't available here; used `git reset --soft HEAD~5` and re-committed as `feat: orders api with validation and tests`.

Pushed `feat/orders-api` and opened a PR with a summary and test plan. CI is running.
CI: lint passed, unit tests passed, e2e passed. Waiting for review.

Regenerated the lockfile with `npm install` after taking main's version, then committed the merge.

What are the trade-offs between OAuth and API keys for production authentication?

OAuth issues short-lived access tokens that can be revoked centrally, and it lets the identity provider enforce multi-factor authentication. API keys are simpler to issue, but they are long-lived, easy to leak into logs, and hard to rotate without downtime. For production authentication the revocation and rotation story matters more than convenience. Operationally OAuth adds a dependency on the identity provider, so an outage there blocks new logins. Teams usually soften that with token caching and a short grace period. The extra setup cost is paid once, while the security benefit compounds over time. In practice most incidents come from leaked long-lived credentials rather than from protocol weaknesses.
